body: Spoken narratives extensively connect moment-to-moment language processing with knowledge accumulated through language and literacy experience. This study examined that relationship using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during Cantonese story listening and contextual representations from large language model (LLM). The imaging cohort comprised 23 school-age children; 16 contributed complete standardized literacy and language assessments and served as held-out participants in a nested cross-subject encoding analysis of the same story. Contextual embeddings predicted distributed narrative responses, with prominent correspondence in temporoparietal and default-network parcels. Regional summaries of the top 25% of voxels ranked by held-out correlation yielded atlas-wide means of r=0.174 and partial R2=0.0165. A joint feature model identified negative surprisal and positive predictive-entropy coefficients across cortical and subcortical parcels, including control, salience, hippocampal and amygdalar regions. Higher word-dictation and overall literacy scores were associated with lower regional encoding performance. Higher Cantonese grammar scores were associated with more negative semantic-update coefficients in parietal control, somatomotor and dorsal-attention parcels. Together, these findings connect language and literacy skills to the regional strength and direction of neural coupling with narrative context. They position naturalistic context processing as a possibly measurable link between oral comprehension and literacy in childhood.
